Go-to-Market Strategy ​

Beachhead: one corridor, not a global launch ​

The temptation in cross-border payments is to claim broad country coverage from day one. The defensible version is narrower: launch in the corridor with the strongest evidence already gathered, prove it works, then expand corridor by corridor.

Based on the research already done in this project (see Potential Partners and Alternative Approaches), Year 1 targets the largest freelancer market in each of three priority regions: Nigeria (Africa), India (Asia), and Brazil (Latin America). All three are corridors the systemic alternatives (UPI-PayNow, Project Nexus, ASEAN mesh) do not reach at the retail freelancer level, since they require a domestic instant-payment system on the receiving end that most of these markets don't yet have linked internationally the way Southeast Asia does.

Launch sequence ​

PhaseFocusExit criterion
1. Three parallel corridorsOne sending country (EU, via SEPA) to Nigeria, India, and Brazil, one payout partner eachA real transfer settles in each corridor, payout confirmed, compliance anchor verifiable on HashScan
2. Corridor depthAdd 2-3 more receiving corridors per region using the same sending-side railPartner agreements signed, not new engineering
3. Second sending marketAdd a second sending country/currency (e.g. UK, GBP)Proves the model isn't EUR-specific
4. Second target segmentExpand from freelancer remittances to general diaspora remittances (the second target market named in Problem Analysis)Volume from segment 2 exceeds a defined threshold relative to segment 1

Each phase is gated on partner agreements, not engineering work. Consistent with the scalability analysis in Business Model: this is a commercially-constrained business, not a technically-constrained one.

Customer acquisition ​

ChannelWhy it fits this specific segment
Freelance platform partnershipsFreelancers already aggregate on platforms; a payout-method integration reaches thousands of users through one partnership, not one user at a time
Diaspora community channelsWhatsApp groups, community associations, and remittance comparison sites are where diaspora senders already research options, not general advertising
Partner co-marketingLicensed payout partners (Yellow Card, MTN MoMo, and equivalents in India/Brazil) have existing user bases; a co-marketing agreement reaches recipients' senders indirectly

What this explicitly avoids: paid general-audience advertising as a first channel. Cross-border remittance senders are price- and trust-sensitive; acquisition in this space works through existing trusted channels (community, platform, partner), not broad awareness campaigns, especially pre-revenue.

Pricing at launch ​

Per Business Model: a transparent flat fee plus a stated FX spread, meaningfully below the global average cost, undercutting the hidden spread most incumbents charge, not necessarily the total cost, since the licensed partners' margins are the majority of the cost regardless of who orchestrates the transfer. The defensible pricing claim at launch is transparency and a real, moderate discount, not being unconditionally cheaper. (The exact discount figure and full unit economics are still being finalized separately.)

What would make this fail ​

Per the same section's own risk framing: a licensed CASP (Due, BVNK) adding a compliance-anchoring layer of their own would remove this project's main differentiation quickly, since they already have the licensing and corridor coverage. The go-to-market bet is that they are optimizing for corridors with existing volume, leaving the corridors this project targets under-served for long enough to establish a partner relationship advantage.
